n_TOF pass 1 · P7a · drift velocity · 17 November 2026

The n_TOF drift velocity follows the weather, not the gas mixer

The drift velocity v of chambers A, C and D was measured for every acquisition of the n_TOF campaign, from how long the charge column of clean tracks lasts. It moves by up to 15 % over the campaign, the three chambers move together, and one smooth shared curve describes it. The gas mixer's own log shows the mix and flow were constant throughout, so the cause is downstream of the mixer. Outdoor humidity and the hall temperature (measured by the ³He capsule and by the mixer's sensor) track it closely, which points to water getting into the gas.

Answer
  • One curve for all chambers: ln v = c[chamber, trigger] + s[chamber]·g(t), with C moving 3.07× and D 2.89× as much as A. Same-sub-run correlation A–C r = 0.85.
  • The mixer did not do it: 9.999 % isobutane (1–99 %: 9.996–10.003) and 7.778 ln/h (7.7775–7.7782) over the whole window, while v moved by percent.
  • Its thermometer helps across long gaps: the mixer's temperature sensor tracks the hall. Added to the smooth model, it makes no difference across 6 h gaps (A / C / D ±1.15 / ±1.50 / ±3.42 % without, ±1.15 / ±1.53 / ±3.24 % with), because the spline already has data on both sides. Across 24 h gaps it takes the error from ±1.38 / ±2.40 / ±3.53 % to ±1.20 / ±1.83 / ±3.08 %, and the pull rms from 1.05 / 1.16 / 1.18 to 1.00 / 1.18 / 1.10 (A and D back to ~1; C's band stays ~20 % narrow across long gaps). The capsule in the same place does about as well for A and C (±1.23 / ±1.80 / ±3.35 %), so what matters is having a hall temperature; the mixer's sensor wins on D. Slope A -0.8 %/K, C -2.4 %/K, D -2.2 %/K: v slows as the hall warms.
  • No rerun: the reconstruction does not use v in the fit; an A/B re-reconstruction of 30 acquisitions with the measured v changes no fit, so the angles are corrected in the tables: tan × v_bundle / v(t).

1. Measuring v per acquisition

A track crossing the 28–29 mm drift gap leaves charge at every depth, and the strips see it arrive over the drift time of the whole gap. Stacking the strip-summed signals of the pass's clean single tracks (≥ 40 per view, not saturated) and fitting the box gives the column duration T, independent of the angle; v = gap / T, x and y views combined. That gives 8,578 acquisition × chamber measurements. B has no field-shaping ring and so no box; D's beam column is not a box, so D is measured on cosmic triggers only. HV never changed during the campaign.

2. A smooth model to interpolate with

v is smooth on the scale of hours: within a ~1 h sub-run acquisitions scatter only a little more than their bootstrap error. The model is a cubic P-spline g(t) shared by the chambers (knots every 2 h, smoothing chosen by cross-validation), plus environmental regressors, fitted on ln v with a per-chamber level and scale. Each chamber gets a jitter term so that χ²/dof = 1, and the spline's covariance gives an interpolation error that grows across gaps. The chambers share one gas line (A → B → C → D), which is why one curve fits all three.

3. The gas mixer was constant

The DAQ's gas_watcher.py logged both Bronkhorst mass-flow controllers every 2 s from 7 July to 10 August (EOS july_beam/slow_control/gas_flow/). Over the v window the setpoint never changed (10.00 % isobutane, argon 7.0 ln/h) and the measured mix held to 0.002 % rms; 0 ten-minute bins lie outside ±0.5 % isobutane or below 7.5 ln/h. A change of a few thousandths of a percent of isobutane cannot move v by percent, so the mixer is ruled out as the driver.

4. What drives v: water and temperature

The outdoor water-vapour pressure (MeteoSwiss Genève-Cointrin), smoothed with a causal 24 h time constant (a model of water permeating into the gas lines), follows the slow trend. The daily wiggle runs opposite to the hall temperature. Two sensors record the hall temperature: the sealed ³He capsule (pressure ∝ temperature) and the mixer's controller. They are correlated but not identical, and the mixer's sensor sits by the gas rack.

Fitting the environment alone (no spline) shows how much each sensor carries:

Both signs are the wrong way for a gas-density (E/N) effect: at this field v would rise with temperature. Instead v falls with water and with temperature, by several %/K on C, far beyond what density could give. Water that enters faster when it is warm and humid (permeation through the lines, outgassing from the walls), and more of it downstream in the chain, fits the signs and the C, D > A ordering. This is a reading of correlations, not a measurement of the gas.

5. Validation

Each model is fitted with part of the data removed and asked to predict it: a random 20 % of acquisitions (interpolation between neighbours), and every 4th block of 6, 12 or 24 h (a real gap: the campaign has accesses and stops of that length). Entries are the 68 % half-width of measured / predicted − 1 in %, with the pull rms in brackets; the row in bold is the model used, chosen by the mean over chambers and the three gap lengths. 6. Does the pass need a rerun? No.

30 beam acquisitions at the fastest times (C 12–15 % above the frozen v, A 3.5–5 %) were re-reconstructed with only the drift velocity changed to the measured one. The fit works in time units: w, p0 and t0 are identical, and tan scales as v_frozen / v. What the frozen v does change is which candidate is ranked first, so about 1 % of tracks are swapped, while the counts change by less than 0.6 %. Decided 17 November: no rerun. tan is corrected in the tables with v(t), |tan| < 0.5 is cut so the acceptance does not move with v, and the ~1 % churn is a stated systematic.

What this does not rule out

  • The water reading is a correlation with outdoor air and two hall thermometers. The mixer log shows what went into the line, not what reached the chambers, and no gas composition was measured during the campaign.
  • The mixer-temperature term is a correlation too. Its weight is fitted, and its gain holds up on held-out 12 and 24 h blocks, but the sensor is a controller's body temperature (it includes self-heating), not a calibrated hall thermometer. Inside normal data taking (gaps under ~6 h) the model is set by the spline and the term changes nothing.
  • A's shape is tied to C's (one curve); A's own small departures (~0.9 %) are in its jitter.
  • D's absolute v reads ~10 % off its bundle even on its own calibration run: its scale needs an angle anchor; only its time dependence is used.
  • v is the column duration over the timing-free gap: a gain change at fixed HV would move T too (HV was constant).
  • The A/B covers beam triggers of A and C; two-track splits were not separated.
